input.question: For higher-rank unitary perturbations, determine which parts of Aronszajn-Donoghue theory survive after the necessary modifications from the rank-one setting, especially when scalar spectral measures are replaced by vector-valued measures.

original_question: For higher-rank unitary perturbations, determine which parts of Aronszajn-Donoghue theory survive after the necessary modifications from the rank-one setting, especially when scalar spectral measures are replaced by vector-valued measures.

original_paper.title: Rank One and Finite Rank Perturbations

rewritten_question: Let U_A be a rank n unitary perturbation of a completely nonunitary contraction U_0, in the model-theoretic setting where the spectral representation uses fibers H(ξ) of dimension up to n and the usual scalar spectral measure is no longer the right object for the singular theory. In the rank-one case, Aronszajn-Donoghue theory says in particular that the singular parts of the spectral measures for different perturbation parameters are mutually singular. For n greater than 1, ordinary scalar mutual singularity cannot be expected to persist. Which parts of rank-one Aronszajn-Donoghue theory still survive for higher-rank unitary perturbations after reformulating the statements in terms of vector-valued or matrix-valued spectral measures, and what is the correct replacement for mutual singularity in that setting?

resolution.status_reason: Later papers from 2019 to 2021 resolve major pieces of the direction by showing that singular-part mutual singularity survives in a vector or matrix-valued form, that scalar mutual singularity survives for almost all perturbations, and that the absolutely continuous part generalizes more directly. But the source question is broader than any one theorem in the later literature, so the bounded search supports a substantial partial resolution rather than one explicit complete closure of the original survey-style question.

search_trace.notes: The bounded later-literature search found two highly relevant follow-up papers by Liaw and collaborators. They establish a matrix-valued replacement for mutual singularity and related almost-every-parameter scalar statements, but they do not present one single theorem explicitly phrased as a complete determination of every surviving component of Aronszajn-Donoghue theory for higher-rank unitary perturbations.

paper_evidence.quote: Rank one unitary perturbations were generalized to higher rank unitary perturbations (for example, in [4, 29]), which describe the situation when the perturbed operator is not cyclic.

Let µA denote the scalar-valued spectral measure; that is, we have the direct integral H = ⊕ ∫T H(ξ)dµA(ξ) with UA = ⊕ ∫T ξ IH(ξ)dµA(ξ). Since D∗ is a cyclic subspace for UA of minimal dimension, we have max dim H(ξ) = n.

Open direction: In the case of higher rank perturbations, we certainly cannot hope that the singular parts of two perturbed operators’ spectral measures are mutually singular. However, it would be interesting to see how much of Aronszajn–Donoghue theory can still be true with appropriate changes in the statements. For example, instead of the scalar spectral measure, one would need to consider vector-valued measures.

Our main result is a generalization of the Aronszajn–Donoghue theorem about the mutual singularity of the singular parts of the spectrum for rank one perturbations to the case of finite rank perturbations. ... we introduce the notion of vector mutual singularity for the matrix-valued measures and show that if we use this notion, the mutual singularity still holds for the finite rank perturbations.

Another interesting result in rank one perturbation theory is the Aleksandrov disintegration theorem... In Theorems 4.2 and 4.6, we prove a version of this result for the case of finite rank perturbations... The matrix version of the Aleksandrov disintegration theorem allows us to get a type of mutual singularity result for singular parts for the scalar spectral measures.

A description of the absolutely continuous parts of µα is a rather straightforward generalization of the well-known results for the scalar case (n = 1). The results and proofs for the singular parts of matrix-valued µα are more complicated than in the scalar case... new phenomena specific to the matrix-valued case appear here. New ideas, including the notion of directionality, are required in statements and proofs.

In scalar Aleksandrov–Clark theory the Aronszajn–Donoghue Theorem [6, 9] states that the singular parts of two distinct measures from the same family must be mutually singular. Trivially, such a statement cannot be true for the matrix-valued measures µsα. However, if one interprets the mutual singularity as the vector mutual singularity introduced in [13], the corresponding result is true, see Corollary 4.6.

difficulty.label: Prerequisite specificity
difficulty.rationale: It depends on specialized perturbation theory, model theory, and matrix-valued spectral-measure technology.

difficulty.label: Domain recognition
difficulty.rationale: The problem lives at the intersection of operator theory, spectral theory, and function-theoretic models, which is not obvious to a broad solver.

difficulty.label: Object unfamiliarity
difficulty.rationale: Vector mutual singularity, matrix-valued Clark measures, and finite-rank perturbation models are unusual objects for most readers.

difficulty.label: Representation setup
difficulty.rationale: One must first choose the correct matrix-valued spectral representation before the question even becomes well posed.

difficulty.label: First foothold visibility
difficulty.rationale: There is no obvious first move unless one already knows that scalar mutual singularity fails and must be replaced.

difficulty.label: Dead-end surface
difficulty.rationale: A natural but wrong path is to search for a literal scalar analogue, which later work shows cannot hold.

difficulty.label: Key leap size
difficulty.rationale: The main leap is replacing scalar singularity by vector mutual singularity and adding directional structure.

difficulty.label: Method novelty
difficulty.rationale: The needed methods go well beyond standard single-measure perturbation arguments.

difficulty.label: Technical length
difficulty.rationale: Even after the right formulation is found, proving the surviving statements requires substantial machinery.

difficulty.label: Computation burden
difficulty.rationale: The challenge is more conceptual and structural than computational.

perfectness.label: Well-posedness and unambiguity

perfectness.label: Solver-fit and self-containedness

perfectness.rationale: The central obstacle is hidden fairly: the scalar statement fails and the correct matrix replacement must be discovered.

perfectness.label: Naturalness of core
